title: 120604-G-JY570-Long-Range-medevac
description: SAN DIEGO -- U.S. Coast Guard and Navy crews work together to medevac an ailing mariner from a merchant vessel approximately 400 miles off the coast of California, June 4, 2012. An MH-60 Jayhawk helicopter crew from San Diego flew to the USS Peleliu to refuel before hoisting the sick man from the cargo ship. U.S. Coast Guard video by Petty Officer 1st Class Henry G. Dunphy.

transcript.text: We decided to send one of our helicopters out to medivac them.
And we worked with the Navy and other coast guard assets
to get to the point where we could extend our range enough
that we could reach them and still have enough fuel
to get back to a Navy ship and then back home to San Diego.
Then he received some initial medical treatment
at the Navy ship that we landed on, the USS Pellow Lou.
And then on Tuesday morning we brought him back to San Diego
for more extensive medical treatment.
So thanks to the coordination of multiple coast guard and Navy units,
we were able to successfully medivac this man from very far offshore
and bring him back to San Diego where he could receive
the necessary medical treatment that he required.
Conducted another trail on delivery to the port bridge wing,
got it on deck, delivered the basket to the bridge wing,
crew members pulled it in, the patient mobile came out of the pilot house,
got into the basket, we retreated the basket,
we retreated the trail line and then departed the scene.
All in all took 10 minutes at the most.
Then once we departed the scene we headed back to the Navy ship,
which point once we landed, medical staff took the patients inside
and gave him a further evaluation and decided that he was not in the medical
need to get medivacs any further last night.
So we ended up staying the night, shutting down,
staying the night aboard the ship.
The USS Peloloo was the LHA where we hot refueled on the way out
and then shut down on the way back.
They allowed us to extend our reach so that way we could get to the man on the ship.
And the other asset was the 1702 out of Sacramento.
Floo was our cover from San Diego to the Peloloo.
And then Floo again, as our cover from the Peloloo out to the Immersion Vessel,
it would cause the communication with them so that way if anything ever happened
or anything changed, they were able to keep an eye on us.
The farthest I've been offshore in a helicopter 400 miles is kind of an area feeling
not being able to see anything or talk to anybody.
